column2: Built to support walls continuously. It usually projects beyond the wall as a cantilever, because the bearing resistance of the ground is lower than that of the masonry, and a placing allowance of at least 5 cm is needed on each side. It is made of brick, rubble stone, rubble or mass concrete, or reinforced concrete.
Under masonry buildings, for example a family house or a smaller block of flats, on bearing ground, below the frost depth. The simplest and cheapest solution.
Under columns and posts

A block footing under the columns; its plan is usually square, B/L = 1–3.5. It is made of concrete or reinforced concrete, with at least a mesh of reinforcement at the bottom. The connection to the column can be fixed or pinned; a precast column today goes into a pocket neck placed on a cast-in-place block footing.
Under the concentrated column loads of framed buildings and industrial halls, if differing settlement of the columns causes no problem.
Reinforced concrete block
Ground beam under a row of columns
The columns are set on a strip-like reinforced concrete beam, usually heavily reinforced. It is in bending, so it is always reinforced concrete; it gives the structure longitudinal stiffness.
On weaker ground or for structural reasons, if unacceptably large differential settlement would develop between the columns in one direction.
Intersecting ground beams
A set of intersecting reinforced concrete beams: it connects the footings in both directions of the column grid.
If the differential settlement has to be reduced in both directions.
A slab running under the whole building

A continuous reinforced concrete structure running under the whole building, supporting walls and columns alike. It is relatively thin, so usually flexible. It can be a flat slab, with downstand or upstand ribs, with hidden ribs, or of the mushroom (flat-slab) type against punching.

If the loads can only be transferred over the full plan area. Under a building with a full basement and high groundwater as an inverted floor, and under buildings of a few storeys also as a ground-bearing slab.
A basement structure acting as a whole
The base slab forms a monolithic whole with the basement walls and floor built on it – structurally a box girder. Very stiff.
Under structures that tolerate only small deformations, most often as the cast-in-place reinforced concrete receiving level of prefabricated panel buildings.
A slab with a curved surface

A mathematically defined surface of single or double curvature in which only normal forces, i.e. tension and compression, develop, no bending. It saves material but needs a lot of labour and time, and strict geometry. The model shows a conical shell under a cylindrical tower.
It is no longer used, because it did not prove economical. A curiosity: the Körszálló hotel in Budapest was also built on a shell foundation.
Quiz – shallow or deep foundation?
When do we call a foundation a shallow foundation?
If the bearing stratum is close to the surface (with a basement, close to the superstructure), within about 1–2 m
If the footing is made of reinforced concrete
If the groundwater level is deep
If the building has at most three storeys
A shallow foundation transfers the load directly to the near-surface bearing stratum. The material, the groundwater or the number of storeys does not decide it on its own.
What is the essence of a deep foundation?
A load-transferring element is inserted between the structure and the deeper bearing ground
The shallow foundation is placed one metre deeper
Piles are always used
The weak soil is replaced over its full thickness
The load-transferring element can be a pile, a diaphragm wall, or a well or caisson foundation. Soil replacement is ground improvement, not a deep foundation.
Which situation does NOT justify a deep foundation?
Risk of scour at a bridge pier in a river
A high groundwater level during construction would make a shallow foundation expensive
The sandy gravel bearing stratum starts at 1.2 m depth, and the settlements are small
A strongly inclined load would create a risk of sliding
A near-surface bearing stratum and small settlement: this is the typical case for a shallow foundation. The other situations listed favour a deep foundation.
Which statement is true for a deepened shallow foundation?
It is built 3–5 m deep with shallow-foundation technology, and designed as a shallow foundation (the shaft resistance is neglected)
The upper, enlarged part of a pile
A basement level surrounded by diaphragm walls
In construction terms it is built in the same way as an ordinary shallow foundation, and its bearing resistance is also calculated with the assumptions used for shallow foundations.
The near-surface layer is weak, but there is nothing better deeper down either, and the loads are moderate. What could be considered?
A raft foundation: the weight of the building is spread over a large area
Only a pile foundation
Smaller pad foundations at closer spacing
It is not possible to build
Exactly this situation: if there is no better layer deeper down either, the load must be spread over a large area.
What is a piled raft?
A mixed (hybrid) system in which the raft and the piles transfer the load together
A raft with temporary piles underneath for the construction period
A pile foundation whose pile cap is slab-shaped
Two separate foundations side by side
For example, the MOL Campus (2.2 m thick raft, 135 piles) and the Burj Khalifa (3.7 m thick raft, 192 piles) stand on one.
Quiz – types of shallow foundation
Why does a strip footing usually project beyond the wall as a cantilever?
Because the bearing resistance of the ground is lower than that of the masonry, and a placing allowance of at least 5 cm is also needed on each side
So that the wall does not settle at all
Because it needs less material
Only for aesthetic reasons
The widening reduces the contact pressure, and the 5 cm on each side covers the inaccuracy of the earthworks.
How should the steps of a brick strip footing be formed?
In height by one course of bricks, horizontally by whole multiples of half a brick
Freely, with a sloping 45° surface
Horizontally by multiples of the brick length
Without steps, always as wide as the wall
This way the bricks can be laid in bond without cutting, and the steps also serve load distribution.
When is a reinforced concrete strip footing advantageous?
If a large bearing area is needed but the depth of the footing is limited (groundwater, basement, etc.)
If the ground is very good
If the wall is thin
If the frost depth is large
The wider an unreinforced footing, the deeper it has to be; a reinforced concrete footing spans the projection with a smaller depth.
What is typical of the plan of a pad foundation?
Usually square, or B/L = 1–3.5
Always circular
Always elongated, B/L > 5
The same as the cross-section of the column
The plan follows the cross-section of the column, most often square.
What is the difference between a continuous beam and a beam-grid foundation?
The continuous beam reduces differential settlement in one direction, the beam grid in both directions
The continuous beam is reinforced concrete, the beam grid is plain concrete
A beam grid is built only under walls
There is no difference
A beam grid consists of intersecting ground beams.
What is a raft with hidden ribs?
One where only additional reinforcement remains where the ribs would be, and the thickness equals that of the ribs
One whose ribs are sunk into the ground
One covered from above by a floor finish
One with a drainage layer underneath
The rib is “hidden”: it is present in the reinforcement of the slab.
Why were box foundations used under prefabricated panel buildings?
Because a building made of prefabricated elements can tolerate only small deformations without damage
Because it is cheaper than a strip foundation
Because the groundwater is always high under panel buildings
Because the panels cannot be fixed to anything else
The cast-in-place receiving level acts as a box girder and makes the foundation stiff.
Quiz – the design process
What must be checked first, before starting to design the foundations?
Whether an adequate ground investigation report is available
How much concrete to order
What colour the plinth should be
Who the contractor will be
Without an adequate ground investigation report, the foundations cannot be designed safely.
What comes directly after setting the foundation level in the flowchart?
Sizing the foundation area in the ultimate limit state
Determining the reinforcement
Checking sliding
Designing a deep foundation
Knowing the foundation level, we determine the required width of the footings (for a raft it is given anyway).
What should be done if the calculated settlements are not acceptable?
Something has to change, and we go back to the start of the design; if necessary, we move to a deep foundation
Increase the concrete grade
Leave out the settlement check
Leave the settlement to the contractor
The type, the foundation level, the footing size – or the whole type of foundation – can be changed.
Which is the last step of the process?
Structural design: choosing the concrete grade and the reinforcement
Setting the foundation level
The settlement calculation
Choosing the foundation type
Before that, the stability of position and the safety against uplift also have to be checked (where relevant).
Which one does NOT belong to the “surroundings” group of factors?
The depth of the groundwater
An adjoining neighbouring building (infill plot)
Trees on the site that must be protected
